conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. It’s not a test of your parenting; it simply gives us a snapshot of how your mood and anxiety have been over the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the right support.

Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. If any question brings up difficult thoughts, we’ll pause and make sure you’re safe and supported.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to look forward to things and enjoy moments, or has that felt harder to do?

I’ve noticed it’s definitely harder. I still get little sparks—like when my baby smiles or when I manage to drink a hot cup of tea—but those moments feel smaller and fade fast. Mostly things that used to excite me just feel flat, like I’m going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really... I mean, every now and then something small will make me crack a smile, but it feels forced, like I have to remind myself "this is supposed to be funny." Most of the time I just feel too tired or down to really laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, not much. I can think of a couple things—like my sister bringing dinner or getting out for a short walk—that I sort of looked forward to, but the excitement is nowhere near what it used to be. Mostly I feel like I’m just getting through the day.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my mind jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I know it’s probably not all on me, but those guilty thoughts keep popping up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding the baby and suddenly my chest feels tight, worrying that he’s too hot or too cold, or that I missed a sign he’s sick—even when everything looks fine. I know the fears don’t always make sense, but I can’t switch them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden panicky feeling—like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath—especially at night when the house is quiet. Nothing specific triggered it; it just hits out of nowhere, and then I lie there imagining worst-case scenarios about the baby.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most days I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff—laundry piles, dishes, trying to soothe the baby while my head’s pounding. Sometimes I manage to push through, but there are moments I just sit on the couch staring, thinking I can’t handle one more thing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind starts spinning—worrying I didn’t burp him right, or replaying every little thing I did wrong—and then I’m wide awake. It can take over an hour to settle, and if he stirs during the night, the same anxious loop starts again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not tears-all-day sad, but there’s this heavy, gray feeling that tags along no matter what I’m doing—like I’m stuck under a cloud while everyone else walks in sunshine.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve broken down twice this week. Once when the baby wouldn’t stop crying and I couldn’t figure out why—I just sat on the nursery floor sobbing. Another time my partner asked how my day was and the question felt so big I burst into tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s crossed my mind a couple of times—just brief flashes, like “what if I weren’t here.” I haven’t thought about how I’d do it or made any plans; the idea just pops in when everything feels too heavy and then disappears. I’m scared to tell anyone, but I don’t want to act on it.

You've shared that over the past week most days feel heavy and gray, with little joy even when your baby smiles. You describe near-daily <sym>anxiety</sym>, sudden <sym>panic</sym>, constant self-blame, and being overwhelmed by ordinary tasks, while <sym>sleep</sym> remains elusive because your mind races with worries about doing motherhood "right." <quote>I just feel too tired or down to really laugh</quote> captures the exhaustion and sadness you're carrying, and you've acknowledged that passive thoughts of not wanting to be here drift in when everything feels too much.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional forced smiles and inability to laugh due to feeling tired or down, matching "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>She reports only "sort of" looking forward to a couple minor things and a clear reduction from her usual enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('I do that a lot') and recurrent guilty thoughts, aligning with 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, irrational worries (temperature, illness) despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panicky episodes multiple times this week with physical symptoms and no clear trigger, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and unable to handle routine tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, captured by "pretty much every day" and the persistent "heavy, gray" mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two clear tearful episodes triggered by ordinary stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent passive suicidal ideation ('crossed my mind a couple of times') without intent or plan, aligning with 'Sometimes'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scores of 12 or higher indicate high probability of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>; at 25, well above that threshold, nearly every item is endorsed at the severe end (Q1-Q9 scored 2-3). She meets screening equivalents of <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>marked loss of interest</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, and <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym> (DSM-5 Criterion A). Q10 score 2 confirms <sym>suicidal ideation</sym>, requiring immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with her <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full diagnostic evaluation and safety plan
2. Call local <med>crisis hotline</med> or 988 if thoughts of self-harm intensify before appointment
3. Inform partner or trusted adult about passive suicidal thoughts and create 24/7 supervision plan for her and baby until professional review
4. Schedule within 48 hours: individual <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>-based therapy session with therapist experienced in <med>postpartum depression</med>
5. Discuss rapid-acting <med>antidepressant</med> options (e.g., SSRIs) and possible starter benefits/breast-feeding compatibility with prescriber
6. Offer practical support: enlist family/friends for night shifts, meal trains, and household tasks to allow at least one 4-hour block of uninterrupted <sym>sleep</sym> daily
7. Provide education materials on <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med>, emphasizing recovery is common with treatment
8. Arrange follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

**Symptoms / Behaviors Reported**  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy gray feeling,” daily tearfulness  
- Marked loss of enjoyment (anhedonia) and anticipatory pleasure  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (“bad mom”)  
- Near-daily, distressing, unprovoked anxiety, panic episodes with somatic symptoms (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Frequent intrusive worries about infant safety  
- Sleep disturbance driven by rumination and hyper-arousal  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” unable to complete routine tasks  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan or intent)

**Pattern**  
Symptoms present most days, present for at least the past week, fluctuate in intensity, interfere with daily functioning and infant care.

**Screening Significance**  
Meets threshold for probable major depressive episode with anxious features; high clinical concern for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder.

**Risk Flags**  
✓ Passive suicidal thoughts → Safety concern  
✓ Impaired functioning, distress, and limited supports noted

**Next Step**  
Recommend immediate comprehensive psychiatric evaluation, safety assessment, and consideration of crisis resources/support services.
